articles.text: Editor: It is my pleasure to write in support of the Piedmont Center of the Arts and the renewal of their lease with the City. Having performed, presented, and attended performances at the PCA, I can say with emphatic certainty that it is a cultural gem in the heart of Piedmont, and I urge you to give them every consideration in this matter. I am a concert pianist, educator, founder and artistic director of the San Francisco International Piano Festival, and active member of arts organization boards throughout the Bay Area including Lieder Alive! and the San Francisco Conservatory’s Presidential Alumni Council. Having performed throughout the country and internationally in addition to dozens of venues throughout the Bay Area, I am particularly grateful for the experiences I have had at the PCA since I first became acquainted with it in 2016. I was invited by Harry Howe, whom I knew through Oakland Symphony, to attend the inaugural season of Piedmont Chamber Music Festival led by the Formosa String Quartet. The level of musicianship was truly first rate, international, and satisfying. It became clear to me that this venue was at the level of the music, and I tucked that experience away in my memory. In 2017, I launched the San Francisco International Piano Festival with support from Piedmont residents Craig and Letitia Casebeer. After establishing ourselves as the only international piano festival in the Bay Area, we chose PCA as the venue for our opening night program in 2018 and 2019. These evenings were great successes on every level, and the setting of the PCA was ideal. Sold-out crowds, open air atmosphere, visual art, and world class piano playing in a warm and approachable environment. I have performed at the PCA myself on a number of occasions and have always found it to be a gratifying experience. As a guest artist with Gold Coast Chamber Players, I played an all-Mozart concert that featured the Alexander String Quartet. The house Steinway is a warm and appropriately sized piano for the space, making it a perfect setting for chamber music both vocal and instrumental, solo piano, and masterclasses. The Center’s programming both visually, musically, and theatrically has contributed enormously to the community, and I look forward to seeing what they will do in their next decade of tenure. I recommend them without hesitation for renewal of their lease and am happy to speak with you directly if I can offer anything further to the process. –Jeffrey LaDeur, Founder, San Francisco Piano Festival
articles.title: In support of PCA lease extension with City

articles.text: A program that lets California residents know if they have been exposed to COVID-19 was made available statewide on December 10. The smartphone application, CA Notify, is available on all iPhones and Android devices. G av i n Ne w s o m announced the launch of CA Notify during a press conference last week when the application officially went live across the “Throughout this pandemic we have tapped California’s talent pool to fight this virus, and that includes working with tech innovators like Apple and Google,” said Gov. Newsom. “CA Notify will help slow the spread by alerting those who opt in to receive an alert if they’ve come into contact with someone who has tested positive. The process is private, anonymous and secure, and is one of the many tools in the state’s data-driven approach to help reduce the spread.” The program is voluntary and is not defined as contact tracing. It notifies users who have been in close contact with another user who has opted into the system and tested positive for the virus. When individuals voluntarily activate CA Notify, the tool uses Bluetooth technology to exchange random codes between phones without revealing the user’s idenIf a CA Notify user tests positive for COVID-19, they will receive a verification code to plug into the app, if they choose. Any other CA Notify users who have been within six feet for 15 minutes or more of the COVID-19 positive individual will get an anonymous notification of possiA new iPhone application alerts users of possible COVID-19 exposure. ble exposure. Users who have tested positive will get a text from the California Department of Public Health with a code, which they can enter into the CA Notify application, triggering an alert to phones of people who may have been exposed in the previous 14 days. Android users can download CA Notify through the application store. Apple iPhone users simply need to activate the built-in feature. It is accessible by enabling “exposure notifications” in the settings area of the device. “When combined with other actions like wearing masks and physical distancing, CA Notify can help curb the transmission of COVID-19,” said Dr. Mark Gahly, California Health and Human Services Secretary. “Every day that is saved in alerting others of a possible exposure, is a day that a possibly infectious person can begin self-quarantine and reduce the spread. This technology is another way for Californians to take proactive steps to keep themselves, their loved ones and their communities safe.” California launched a pilot of CA Notify in September for university students, staff and faculty at UC San Diego and UC San Francisco, and then later to other UC campuses in mid-November. The university system estimates that more than 250,000 people are now utilizing the application and technology. “Our pilot experience starting at UC San Diego and expanding to other UC campuses showed this technology was effective in identifying exposed individuals early for quarantine and testing, and helping keep our communities as safe as possible,” said Christopher Longhurst, MD, chief information officer of UC San Diego Health. “This free and reliable smartphone technology can help all Californians. As we enter a new, and hopefully final, surge in the pandemic, now more than ever is the time to put every possible tool to use to slow the spread of the virus.” For more information, see: CaNotify.ca.gov and Covid19. ca.gov.

articles.text: UCSF epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford. The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host another virtual forum with internationally renowned epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford on Wednesday, January 13 at 4 p.m. Rutherford last spoke at a LWV forum in May and answered questions on the efficacy of mask-wearing and vaccine availability. Next week’s forum aims to explore the epidemiologist’s predictions for the course of the COVID-19 virus in 2021 and answer questions about availability and distribution of the vaccine. Rutherford, a Piedmont resident, has been instrumental in keeping the Bay Area abreast on COVID-19 related concerns and is quoted as an expert source in nationwide media outlets. The virtual forum is entitled “COVID-19 Update: Are We Any Closer to the End?” and will focus on when life can return to “normal” after nearly a year of lockdowns. There will be a question-and-answer portion of the forum after a presentation. Viewers can submit their own questions directly in the forum. Rutherford leads the Global Strategic Information group within University of California (UCSF), San Francisco’s Institute for Global Health Sciences. He is the Salvatore Pablo Lucia Professor of Epidemiology, Preventive Medicine, Pediatrics and History; Head of the Division of Infectious Disease and Global Epidemiology in the Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics in School of Medicine at UCSF and Professor of Epidemiology and Health Administration in the School of Public Health at the University of California, Berkeley. Registration is not required for the event. The smartphone application, CA Notify, is available on all iPhones and Android devices. G ov. G av i n Ne w s o m announced the launch of CA Notify during a press conference last week when the application officially went live across the state. “Throughout this pandemic we have tapped California’s talent pool to fight this virus, and that includes working with tech innovators like Apple and Google,” said Gov. Newsom. “CA Notify will help slow the spread by alerting those who opt in to receive an alert if they’ve come into contact with someone who has tested positive. The process is private, anonymous and secure, and is one of the many tools in the state’s data-driven approach to help reduce the spread.” The program is voluntary and is not defined as contact tracing. It notifies users who have been in close contact with another user who has opted into the system and tested positive for the virus. When individuals voluntarily activate CA Notify, the tool uses Bluetooth technology to exchange random codes between phones without revealing the user’s identity or location. If a CA Notify user tests positive for COVID-19, they will receive a verification code to plug into the app, if they choose. Any other CA Notify users who have been within six feet for 15 minutes or more of the COVID-19 positive individual will get an anonymous notification of possiA new iPhone application alerts users of possible COVID-19 exposure. ble exposure. Users who have tested positive will get a text from the California Department of Public Health with a code, which they can enter into the CA Notify application, triggering an alert to phones of people who may have been exposed in the previous 14 days. Android users can download CA Notify through the application store. Apple iPhone users simply need to activate the built-in feature. It is accessible by enabling “exposure notifications” in the settings area of the device. “When combined with other actions like wearing masks and physical distancing, CA Notify can help curb the transmission of COVID-19,” said Dr. Mark Gahly, California Health and Human Services Secretary. “Every day that is saved in alerting others of a possible exposure, is a day that a possibly infectious person can begin self-quarantine and reduce the spread. This technology is another way for Californians to take proactive steps to keep themselves, their loved ones and their communities safe.” California launched a pilot of CA Notify in September for university students, staff and faculty at UC San Diego and UC San Francisco, and then later to other UC campuses in mid-November. The university system estimates that more than 250,000 people are now utilizing the application and technology. “Our pilot experience starting at UC San Diego and expanding to other UC campuses showed this technology was effective in identifying exposed individuals early for quarantine and testing, and helping keep our communities as safe as possible,” said Christopher Longhurst, MD, chief information officer of UC San Diego Health. “This free and reliable smartphone technology can help all Californians. As we enter a new, and hopefully final, surge in the pandemic, now more than ever is the time to put every possible tool to use to slow the spread of the virus.” For more information, see: CaNotify.ca.gov and Covid19. ca.gov. By Allyson Aleksey The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host another virtual forum with internationally renowned epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford on Wednesday, January 13 at 4 p.m. Rutherford last spoke at a LWV forum in May and answered questions on the efficacy of mask-wearing and vaccine availability. Next week’s forum aims to explore the epidemiologist’s predictions for the course of the COVID-19 virus in 2021 and answer questions about availability and distribution of the vaccine. Rutherford, a Piedmont resident, has been instrumental in keeping the Bay Area abreast on COVID-19 related concerns and is quoted as an expert source in nationwide media outlets. The virtual forum is entitled “COVID-19 Update: Are We Any Closer to the End?” and will focus on when life can return to “normal” after nearly a year of lockdowns. There will be a question-and-answer portion of the forum after a presentation. Viewers can submit their own questions directly in the forum. Rutherford leads the Global Strategic Information group within University of California (UCSF), San Francisco’s Institute for Global Health Sciences. He is the Salvatore Pablo Lucia Professor of Epidemiology, Preventive Medicine, Pediatrics and History; Head of the Division of Infectious Disease and Global Epidemiology in the Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics in School of Medicine at UCSF and Professor of Epidemiology and Health Administration in the School of Public Health at the University of California, Berkeley. The program opened on December 30, and thousands of applications have been received since then. articles.text: Film directors Nicole Newnham and Jim LeBrecht. No one at Camp Jened could’ve imagined that those summers in the woods together would be the beginnings of a revolution. Just down the road from Woodstock, Camp Jened was a camp for disabled teens. Directors Nicole Newnham, a local resident who lives near Piedmont Avenue, and Jim LeBrecht deliver a rousing film about a group of campers turned activists who shaped the future of the disability rights movement and changed accessibility legislation for everyone. Filled with the spirit, music, and humor of the era, Newnham and LeBrecht speak firsthand to the seeds of empowerment that were planted at Camp Jened. Footage from 1971 captures how the campers were finally seen beyond their disabilities. Milestones in the disability-rights movement intersect with LeBrecht’s personal story and the stories of several Camp Jened alums, including then-counselor Judy Heumann. She went on to play an indispensable role in historic protests leading to the Americans with Disabilities Act. Crip Camp shines a bright light on an overlooked civil-rights battle. Crip Camp acquires breadth and seriousness that neither its early scenes nor its playfully confrontational title suggest. As we follow campers into direct actions, occupations and unsparing encounters with government officials, the film’s approach remains anecdotal and emotional. Footage of a twenty-something Judy Heumann reproaching Eugene Eidenberg from the U.S. Department of Health is a master class in focused, righteous rage. Heumann went on to advise Presidents Clinton and Obama. Crip Camp opened the Sundance Film Festival and took home the Audience Award as Best Documentary. The film was produced by Barack and Michelle Obama under their production company Higher Ground. Samples of questions asked on a mental health survey sent to all Piedmont students in September last year. Results were not flattering and were discussed publicly only on December 15. which they were asked to identify one of four pictures depicting their mood. For example, in school connectedness, one question was “I am treated with respect at my school.” Students in grades 6-12 were able to respond by selecting: Almost always, Often, Sometimes, or Never. Student responses were scored by Piedmont school psychologists and “normed” at UC Berkeley. Students scoring in the highest one-sixth of responses were defined as “at-risk,” and the top one percentile were deemed “clinically significant.” The Student Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire found that approximately 14 percent of elementary school students registered in the at-risk category, and less than 1 percent of responses were deemed clinically significant. At Piedmont Middle School, approximately 13 percent of the student responses fell into the category of at-risk, but four percent showed the very troubling results defined as clinically significant. At Millennium High where 46 students took the survey, 14 percent were deemed at-risk and 2 percent were clinically significant. PHS found 13 percent of students tested as at-risk while 3 percent scoring as clinically significant. Joy of Learning and School Connectedness showed up as the biggest concerns at both Havens and Wildwood Elementary schools. Part Two The second part of the survey used a different surveying instrument, called Youth Internalizing and Externalizing Problems Screener (YIEPS). Its goal was to help understand how students are processing and expressing stress caused by: Pandemic Online classes Altered social lives Externalizing Externalizing was defined as externally-focused behavioral symptoms including aggression, problems of conduct, something called “oppositionality,” hyper activity, and problems of attention. Ten questions were asked to calculate the degree to which students are acting out their struggles. Among elementary students, 15 percent fell into the at-risk category for externalizing but with no clinically significant results. At the middle school (grades 6-8) externalizing surveys found 12 percent to be at-risk and 6 percent of students falling into the clinically significant category. Millennium’s externalizing survey showed that 17 percent were at-risk and 4 percent were clinically significant. Results among Piedmont High School students indicated that 10 percent of all students were at-risk, and 5 percent were clinically significant. Internalizing Ten more questions were designed to understand internally-focused behavior, such as: • being nervous or irritable • being withdrawn • eating more or less than usual • feeling sad, lonely or afraid These questions were not asked of elementary school students. Results from the middle school showed that 15 percent were at-risk, and 5 percent were clinically significant. Millennium results recorded a total of 22 percent of its students internalizing at an at-risk level and 4 percent clinically significant. Piedmont High had 14 percent of its student in the at-risk category for internalizing, and 4 percent classified as clinically significant. “There are definitely more students in the at-risk category than had been expected,” said Curriculum Director Wozniak. The most concerning item and biggest takeaway from the screener was the acknowledgement of the levels of “clinically significant” results, which the district had anticipated to only be 1 percent. The initial presentation to school board members on December 15 was murky and lacked clarity. Wozniak apologized at the end of the presentation. “It was late afternoon that I found out I was going to be the one explaining the data points. I of course had looked at [them], but not at any way close to the level the school psychologists had been studying these. I apologize for the lack of clarity in some of these explanations,” she said. “[The screener results are] exactly what we have been afraid of. I don’t know how it is going to unfold, but what we definitely need to do is find creative ways to bring our kids together in some kind of in-person communities in some way, even if it is not necessarily in a classroom,” said board member Amal Smith. Since the survey was non-confidential, counselors and teachers have been able to contact students and parents about the troubling responses. The counselors at each school have their hands full. “The truth is, [with] these numbers and only 40 percent FTE [full-time employees] at Beach and Wildwood [for counselors], you just cannot service and meet with students one on one every week,” she said. Board Vice-President Megan Pillsbury brought up a caveat to the non-confidential nature of the screener. “I was curious how it was framed, to the high school students especially. What were students told in regards to how and what questions were going to be used? I am just thinking with high school students, they would be savvy about ‘what are you trying to get at here?’,” Pillsbury said. Because students’ names were recorded on the surveys, a question to be asked could be if students “internalized” their stress on the screener itself and did not report it. MHS principal Shannon Fierro, who has been reviewing and coding the raw data for her students, said she does not see the lack of anonymity as a concern, but as a strength. “I do not get the sense that because students knew the data was connected to them, that broadly they shied away from being honest about it. There were quite a few students that were endorsing high levels of stress, anxiety and depression. It seems they were kind of saying, ‘Yeah, thanks for asking, come talk to me about it’,” Fierro said. Overall, a major concern is the delay in reporting the numbers to the public and to students and parents. Why did it take more than two months to tally, analyze and report the data? The school board specifically made a priority of social-emotional and mental health when they revised the Learning Continuity Plan for this year. Now January, over three months after the survey was sent and with California now the epicenter of the pandemic, Piedmont families are still waiting for a comprehensive explanation from the School Superintendent and Curriculum Director on the depth of the mental health problems affecting students throughout the district. The screener will be given out again in January or February, and another time in the spring. READ IT IN THE POST

On December 31, Chabot Space and Science Center continued its 20-year tradition of a New Year’s Eve Balloon Drop. This time however, the festivities took place on Zoom. In prior years balloons would fall from Chabot’s entry way atrium every hour celebrating January 1 across the globe. Kids would line up and count down until the top of each hour inundated them with balloons cascading from above. This year 160 families tuned into the event, which took place from 11 a.m. to 12 noon on Thursday, December 31. The celebration culminated as a half world away, people in Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan were celebrating the first day of 2021. When the clock struck 12:00 hundreds of colorful, biodegradable balloons rained down from above for participants to watch on their screens. To spice up the event, noise makers, bubbles and a STEM Activity Kit was shipped to registered participants. Virtual Activity Guides were also included with all tickets purchased. Chabot New Year’s Eve revelers got to participate in many activities on the final day of 2020. Chabot’s High School Galaxy Explorers led a Solar Modeling activity, a Mars Lander activity and a Build your own Catapult activity. Nano@Stanford also conducted a magnet activity. Fun was had by all and time flew by, so much so that a couple of activities needed to be saved for the new year. The activity

articles.text: OTR/L January marks the midway point for the 2020-2021 school calendar. This is a perfect time to revisit your student’s home workspace as the continuation of some form of distance learning is highly likely. Setting up the best workspace both from an ergonomic and sensory framework will support participation and success. Dedicated work space First and foremost, does your student have a dedicated workspace? From my observations during classroom synchronized lessons, the majority of students have a dedicated and appropriate workspace. However, popups of couches and coffee tables as workspaces are occasionally seen. Best practice is to always work at a desk, folding table or kitchen/dining table as this alerts the brain that it is “work time” and not “chill time.” Furniture Second, how does the chair and desk/table fit? Poor posture as a result of an ill fit can lead to fatigue and discomfort which ultimately adversely impacts attention and focus. Remember hips, knees and elbows at 90-90-90. When seated, feet should be flat on the floor with knees and hips at 90 degrees. If feet are dangling, posture is compromised. A footstool or stacked books can do the trick. Forearms should rest on the tabletop with elbows at or slightly near a 90-degree angle. And ideally, the computer screen should be at eye level to prevent neck strain. Students can elevate their Chromebooks on a cardboard box when viewing a class. Investing in an external keyboard will allow the Chromebook to remain at eye level while working. Finding the best chair Third, students are now sitting for prolonged periods of time. Finding the right seating option for support and comfort is a must. Office chairs are an easy answer. They offer an adjustable height, cushion and back support and they swivel and rock for those that need more movement for self-regulation. For a regular straight back chair, consider purchasing a seat cushion designed to address both improved posture and comfort. Examples include the highly rated grid seat cushion by Purple and the Tempur-Pedic Memory Foam seat. However, regular straightbacked chairs are easily outfitted with pillows for comfort and height adjustment. Finally, take time to examine the sensory environment that your student is working in by completing an Environmental Sensory Scan. This will help to identify and remedy any sensory challenges that may be present. Environmental sensory stimuli, such as visual or auditory input, can be overwhelming, making your student work harder to process, organize and adapt to the external sensory input before they can even attempt to attend a synchronized class lesson. With your student, sit in the space and notice by looking and listening. What do they hear in the room, a nearby room or outside? What do they notice visually? For example, lighting, clutter or the level of activity in the room? Identify what is distracting and/or bothersome and make changes to the sensory environment. Examples of simple environmental auditory and visual sensory strategies include: external headphones; set Chromebook volume to preferred level; close windows or adjacent door; adjust natural and/or artificial lighting sources; use a cardboard trifold barrier; face the desk toward a wall; reduce visual clutter on and around workspace. With these tips and strategies, let’s welcome 2021 with renewed spirits and an ergonomic and sensory smart workspace that supports participation and success! Kimberly Bonacum is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional questions, she can be contacted at mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com.

articles.text: I can’t wait till I have kids and they start learning about 2020 and ask me all kind of questions. That’s when I’ll just stare off into the distance and begin my story, while my husband sits in the back nodding slowly and occasionally adding a random fact. They’ll have to read an entire textbook on 2020, because we all know that a section isn’t going to cover everything about the historic year. I can imagine some of the questions on tests: What happened in 2020? 1) Murder hornets 2) California and Australia nearly burned to the ground 3) A pandemic halted the world 4) An American president tried to overturn election results 5) All of the above. At least that god-awful year is over. Going into 2021 isn’t going to fix our problems, but the way I look at it, we have a clean slate – a chance to start over. Thanks to the power of the people we got Joseph Biden as our 46th president. Now with a new federal government we at least have a renewed hope for a solid COVID task force that relies on science and experience. But no matter how good he might be, the president alone can’t make all our problems go away. Everyone needs to do their part to help bring the U.S. back to the stature it used to have in the world. First of all, we need to face the oncoming climate crisis that could potentially be devastating to the planet and the human race. Look around you. It’s December in California and you can walk around in lightweight clothing and not be cold. Right now, we should be having rain all the time, but it’s only rained three times since summer. We can do our part to reverse climate change by making small changes in our everyday lives. For example, we can stop buying fast fashion because it uses huge amounts of fossil fuel to make the clothes, and it generates hundreds of thousands of pounds of trash. You can support local businesses because they don’t need to transport their goods from halfway across the world, generating massive amounts of pollution. You can refuse to buy goods from companies that are known to be hurting our environment. Just google and the list will come up. You can also support an environmental cause like Saving the Arctic. The Arctic is in danger of being one of the last safe havens for animals as it is exploited for oil. You can help by signing a petition to help stop this. Go to protectthearctic.org and do your part to help. Another thing that you can do is take action for a cause you believe in. For instance, if you have a cause, you can start a club at school. No drastic measures are required for there to be an impact. You could even make posters and hang them around your school to show your support. Even the smallest change can help. Although 2020 seemed like a year without any good moments, it showed us that there are so many things that need to be fixed. It showed us how bad things had gotten over the last decade in terms of the climate, racial issues, and political controversies. But as Gen Z, it’s up to us to step up and take charge of our future. I believe we have everything it takes to make a world that is safe and stable. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.
articles.title: Look out, 2021 – here we come

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. But Niners’ fans’ minds are likely less focused on who will command its talented young group of defenders and more concentrated on how coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch will approach the freeagent market and 2021 NFL Draft. As we had said throughout the season, the elephant in the room is quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo. We’re not doubting Shanahan, who already declared Jimmy G his starter for next season, but the draft is certainly a high likelihood for SF. Garoppolo’s $25 million salary in 2021 makes him an obvious restructure candidate given the 49ers’ only have $20 million in cap space and have several pricey free-agents set to hit the market, like left tackle Trent Williams, cornerback Richard Sherman, defensive end Solomon Thomas, safety Jaquiski Tartt, and running backs Tevin Coleman and Jeff Wilson. The 49ers are likely to only sign Williams, and possibly one more of their impending freeagents, like Thomas. Signing a free-agent quarterback to compete with Garoppolo doesn’t make sense. Sitting at No. 12 overall in the 2021 NFL Draft doesn’t do San Francisco many favors when considering their options at quarterback. The top three college quarterbacks – Clemson’s Trevor Lawrence, Ohio State’s Justin Fields, and BYU’s Zach Wilson – should be off the board by the time the 49ers have their pick at No. 12. That leaves North Dakota State’s Trey Lance as the logical suit for the 49ers, but it could require Lynch trading up into the top-10 to grab him. The 49ers only have one second-round pick and none in the third round, meaning not much capital is available at this moment. However, SF will gain a thirdround pick for Sherman once he signs with a new team on the open market, while Thomas and Tartt could land contracts that would award third-round compensatory selections as well—which could become trade-bait for the 49ers’ front office. A wildcard option? The Jets may listen to lowball offers for quarterback Sam Darnold, who has a year left on his rookie contract. Gus Bradley, Falcons’ interim HC Raheem Morris, and Rams’ assistant Joe Barry. Coach Jon Gruden showed he’s still an offensive guru. articles.text: The California Interscholastic Federation (CIF) announced on Tuesday, January 5 its intention to produce a plan for high school sports competition by January 25. The announcement was not accompanied by any definitive plan. All high school spors in California has been discontiued since August due to COVID-19. The State declared that some sports can start as planned for counties in the widespread Purple Tier. Those sports would include Cross Country, Tennis, Golf, Swimming, and Track & Field. This means that the cross country program will be the first sport to return. It currently is the only sport given clearance. Tennis, golf, swimming, and track are scheduled for Season 2, from March to June. Under the current CIF framework, cross country would behin competition on January 27 and the season would run until March 27. However, both the North Coast section championship meet at Haywards High and th eState Meet in Fresno have been canceled. “Everyone in California wants students to be able to return to in-person learning, sports, and all other co-curricular activities that are so important for their physical and mental wellbeing,” wrote CIF executive director Ronald Nocetti in a press release. “As COVID-19 transmission rates are rising significantly in California, communities across the state must continue to take measures to limit the spread of the virus. This is the way to ensure the best chance for CIF competition to commence by January 25, as allowed by the guidance from the California Department of Public Health. State agencies will continue to monitor epidemiological trends.” The CIF gave its first indication since March 2020 that inter-scholastic competition will be permitted. For Cross Country, that means events between schools will be allowed if both teams are located in Alameda County or on bordering counties—meaning PHS should be eligible to compete with schools from Contra Costa County, San Mateo County, Marin County, and Santa Clara County if they gain clearance. “Competitions, meets, races, or similar events are authorized only if (a) both teams are located in the same county and the sport is authorized, or (b) teams are located in immediately bordering counties and the sport is authorized in both counties,” wrote the CIF. The CIF also intends on amending rules for cross country, swimming, and golf to allow events with more than two schools. “Any tournaments or events that involve more than two teams are not currently permitted in California. Exceptions may be made, with authorization from the local health department, for the following sports where individual competitors from multiple teams are routine: track and field; cross-country; golf; skiing and snowboarding; tennis; and swimming/diving,” announced the CIF.

articles.text: Big Basin State Park’s relief efforts were given a big boost with Sempervirens Fund and Save the Redwoods League announcing that they have raised $543,000 in donations to help the park’s restoration following the devastating CZU Complex fire in August. Both organizations have supported Big Basin, California’s oldest state park, since its founding in 1902. On Decemer 26 they jointly announced that $200,000 will be directed toward staffing and equipment costs for removing trees deemed hazardous. “State Parks is grateful for this outpouring of support and the ongoing partnership with people who care so deeply about Big Basin,” said Chris Spohrer, Santa Cruz District Superintendent for California State Parks. “This initial funding will allow us to access the backcountry, inventory damages, continue hazard mitigation and take the first steps toward recovery.” Park officials added that the first phase of their recovery operation will allow them to prepare for winter storms, and allow deeper access to evaluate the total damage caused by the wildfire. “We are eager to visit Big Basin again, and that begins with clearing the way for a safe park to emerge from the wildfire’s aftermath,” said Sempervirens Fund executive director Sara Barth. “State parks can be lighter on the land, have more resilient infrastructure and be Photo courtesy of Los Angeles Times An initial $200,000 endowment will go toward removing hazardous trees in Big Basin State Park. Photo courtesy of San Mateo County The CZU Complex fire covered 86,509 acres of the San Mateo and Santa Cruz mountains. Photo courtesy of Sempervirens.org The Sempervirens Fund and Save the Redwoods League raised $543,000 for the restoration of Big Basin State Park which was severely damaged during the CZU Complex fire in August. welcoming and inclusive for all, and Big Basin can lead the way. We are grateful for the generosity of our donors, and to Save the Redwoods League for joining us in this effort and to California State Parks for their thoughtful approach to recovery,” she said. The 86,509-acre wildfire destroyed nearly all the buildings and campgrounds in Big Basin State Park, including its historic Ranger Station and Visitor Center. The funding will help rebuild facilities and operations. In November, park officials stated that it will take at least one year merely to determine the full scope of damage and plan for cleanup projects. “Bridges are out, trees are down across trails, hazard trees are being identified. Access is extremely difficult,” said California State Parks senior environmental scientist Joanne Kerbavaz. Specialists have mentioned time and again that the fire will enable heat-sensitive pine cones to sprout seeds. Although some redwood trees have been destroyed, the bark provided a natural resilience to the blaze. Save the Redwoods League CEO Sam Hodder said that given the larger picture, Big Basin’s trees are doing well. “We are encouraged by the resilience that the redwood forest in Big Basin is already showing,” he said. “We look forward to working closely with our longtime partners Sempervirens Fund and California State Parks to reimagine and rebuild the state’s original redwood park for a 21st-century California – to create a visitor experience that will be welcoming and resonant to our full community.” For more information on the Big Basin State Park recovery fund, visit www.Sempervirens. org/redwoods-recovery.

articles.text: Songs for a New World, filmed on stage at San Francisco Playhouse and presented as an on-demand video stream, will be available only through January 15. The play is about “hitting the wall and having to make a choice, or take a stand, or turn around and go back.” It is the first musical from Tony award-winning playwright Jason Robert Brown and is a moving collection of powerful songs that examine life, love, and the choices people make. Brown has been hailed as “one of Broadway’s smartest and most sophisticated songwriters since Stephen Sondheim” (Philadelphia Inquirer), and his “extraordinary, jubilant theater music” (Chicago Tribune) has been heard all over the world, whether in one of the hundreds of productions of his musicals every year or in his own live performances. The New York Times described Brown as “a leading member of a new generation of composers who embody high hopes for the American musical.” The play is directed by Bill English, with choreography by Nicole Helfer. Songs for a New World features cast members John Paul Gonzalez, Cate Hayman, Rodney Earl Jackson Jr., and Katrina Lauren McGraw. The play premiered on December 12. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2020-2021-season/songs-for-a-new-world/ for program information and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: SF Playhouse’s Songs for a New World ends on January 15

articles.text: Edwin Outwater, Music Director of San Francisco Conservatory of Music, is the subject of a documentary film to be shown on Friday, January 8 at 7:30 p.m. What We Do on the Stage, a documentary concert film envisioned by San Francisco Conservatory of Music and its Music Director Edwin Outwater, will premiere this Friday, January 8 at 7:30 p.m. The documentary follows Outwater and his students as they explore what it means to perform on a stage for an audience and how that paradigm has evolved during the pandemic. The program includes works by Pauline Oliveros (Sonic Meditation VII), Samuel Barber (Mutations on Bach), Mozart (Gran Partita), Morton Feldman (Madame Press Died Last Week at Ninety) and more. The documentary will allow audiences to experience firsthand the advantages of playing in a large ensemble. You will also get a complete overview of orchestral repertoire, beginning with masterworks and then delving into lesser-known pieces of every era. To reserve a spot to view the film, visit https://sfcm.edu/performance-calendar/event/sfcmorchestra-conducted-edwin-outwater-1.
articles.title: SF Conservatory documentary concert film this Friday

articles.text: Joon-ho Bong’s highly satirical movie, Parasite, is the first non-english language film to win the Academy Award for best picture. Movie review by Chris Honoré Winner of the Best Feature at the 2019 Academy Awards, Parasite is many things – a satire, a dark comedy, ambiguous to a fault, ever enigmatic, and a sendup of social inequality. It’s also persistently perplexing. Even when the narrative seems clearly framed it abruptly shifts in tone and direction, forcing the audience to pause and reconsider the meaning of the latest reveal. What Parasite is not is a horror film, its title referring to larger social norms and values, focusing on the differences between classes. In this case it is two families, each living in Seoul, in starkly different circumstances. The story opens with the Kim family: father, Ki-woo (Song Kang-ho), mother, Chung-sook (Jang Hye-jin), son, Ki-woo (Choi Woo-shik) and daughter, Ki-jung (Park So-dam). They live in a small rabbit-warren apartment below street level, bug infested, where they are able to get wi-fi only by using a neighbor’s signal while sitting on an elevated toilet in their one bathroom. Their meager income is derived from folding pizza boxes for a local business. It’s at this point that the story subtly shifts. The Kim son, Ki-woo, meets a friend who asks for a favor: while he is away, would he tutor the teenage daughter of the Park family, Da-hye (Jung Ji-so)? Ki-woo agrees. The following day he finds himself being interviewed by the mother, Yeon-kyo (Jo Yeo-jeong), who is desperate to find someone to help Da-hye with her lessons. Ki-woo is astonished by the house, a walled-in contemporary, spacious, elegant. It is clear that the Park family is affluent. The father, Dong-ik (Lee Sunkyun), is the owner of a successful IT firm. The Parks have a much younger son, Da-song (Jung Hyun-jun) who Yeon-kyo indulges in all ways and is convinced he could benefit from art lessons. Hired on the spot, Ki-woo meets Da-hye and supervises her first lesson and soon leaves. Later he sits with his own family and explains his good fortune. He mentions that the mother wants art lessons for the small boy and he has told the mother that his sister is schooled in art and perhaps she might be willing to instruct Da-song. Eager to have the boy occupied, the mother is grateful. And when Ki-woo returns for another lesson, he brings Ki-jung with him. It becomes apparent that the Kims are small-time grifters and they see an opportunity. Dong-ik has a driver. Get rid of him and Ki-woo can recommend Ki-taek for the position. The Parks also have a housekeeper (Lee Jeongeun). Cause her to be released and recommend the Kim mother, Chung–sook (Jang Hye-jin). And within a week or two, the entire Kim family is working for the Parks who are unaaware of the familial connections. It’s at this point that the story takes another turn. The Kims are astonished at their luck, realizing that their sudden wealth and positions are, as Chung-sook says, akin to an iron, which can smooth out all the wrinkles that once plagued them. But of course this is just the middle of act two and when the Parks leave for a long camping weekend, the Kims, of course, take up residence, feeling very much at home, lounging in the living room, food covering the furniture. What could go wrong? Can this charade end well? Writer/director Boon Jong-ho is eager to answer that question, and so the story takes yet another turn that is completely unanticipated. While the family is relaxing, the hour late, the house theirs to enjoy, the doorbell rings. They quickly learn that it’s the recently released housekeeper who has come to retrieve something she insists she left behind when she so hurriedly departed. Beyond this point that it’s best to drop any discussion of plot, for the story again changes, while a strange new twist is introduced. What Parasite does not do is cast either the Kims or the Parks as stereotypes. Each family is in its own way likable and in its own ways insulated by their social and economic situations. Either could have been foils and Joon-ho avoids that trap. How this all unfolds and resolves itself – its startling climax and quiet denouement – represent the true pleasure of watching what proves to be a truly unique and entertaining film. Parasite. Directed by Joon-ho Bong. Starring Song Kang-ho, Jo Jeo-jong and So-dam Park, With subtitles. 2 hrs., 12 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Parasite – Academy Award- winner as best film

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré While waiting for the moment when I can walk into a theater and spend two hours watching a movie with strangers, I wait. In the interim, I watch movies on a much smaller screen. Many, if not most, I have seen before. I’ve come to realize that seeing a film twice, maybe three times, can be more than interesting. Good movies are layered, can be deeply subtle, with small moments missed on the first viewing. That was my experience with The Book of Henry, which I first watched when it was released in 2017. The critics were almost unanimously harsh in their reviews. I recalled genuinely liking it. I just didn’t remember why. So, I watched with interest, trying to understand what there was about Henry that caused it to be so stridently judged. I watched it again the next day, and the day after that. My reaction to Henry was that I found it for many reasons to be extraordinary. Put simply, I loved it. The characters were beautifully rendered, beginning with Henry (Jaeden Lieberher), his younger brother, Peter (Jacob Tremblay, and his mother, Susan (Naomi Watts). Their individual performances were remarkable, inspired, with moments that bordered on the wondrous. (I’m thinking of one scene when Henry is in the hospital and Peter sits at the foot of his bed and they discuss what lies ahead). After three viewings I came to understand that Henry is a meditation on the remarkable connections that can define family. This film is magical realism; what takes place, especially in the second half, requires a willing suspension of disbelief. What the movie does is submerge the audience in a deeply moving story which is an aggregate of wonderful moments that resonate. They are filled with a tenderness and honesty that are both magical and clearly beyond that cranky cohort of critics bound by literalism. The character who gives the film its narrative structure is, of course, Henry. Introduced in the first act of the film we see that he is deeply smart (with a shrug he says he prefers precocious). Jaeden Martell (Lieberher) as Henry Carpenter in The Book of Henry. Joon-ho Bong’s highly satirical movie, Parasite, is the first non-english language film to win the Academy Award for best picture. Movie review by Chris Honoré Winner of the Best Feature at the 2019 Academy Awards, Parasite is many things – a satire, a dark comedy, ambiguous to a fault, ever enigmatic, and a sendup of social inequality. It’s also persistently perplexing. Even when the narrative seems clearly framed it abruptly shifts in tone and direction, forcing the audience to pause and reconsider the meaning of the latest reveal. What Parasite is not is a horror film, its title referring to larger social norms and values, focusing on the differences between classes. In this case it is two families, each living in Seoul, in starkly different circumstances. The story opens with the Kim family: father, Ki-woo (Song Kang-ho), mother, Chung-sook (Jang Hye-jin), son, Ki-woo (Choi Woo-shik) and daughter, Ki-jung (Park So-dam). They live in a small rabbit-warren apartment below street level, bug infested, where they are able to get wi-fi only by using a neighbor’s signal while sitting on an elevated toilet in their one bathroom. Their meager income is derived from folding pizza boxes for a local business. It’s at this point that the story subtly shifts. The Kim son, Ki-woo, meets a friend who asks for a favor: while he is away, would he tutor the teenage daughter of the Park family, Da-hye (Jung Ji-so)? Ki-woo agrees. The following day he finds himself being interviewed by the mother, Yeon-kyo (Jo Yeo-jeong), who is desperate to find someone to help Da-hye with her lessons. Ki-woo is astonished by the house, a walled-in contemporary, spacious, elegant. It is clear that the Park family is affluent. The father, Dong-ik (Lee Sunkyun), is the owner of a successful IT firm. The Parks have a much younger son, Da-song (Jung Hyun-jun) who Yeon-kyo indulges in all ways and is convinced he could benefit from art lessons. Hired on the spot, Ki-woo meets Da-hye and supervises her first lesson and soon leaves. Later he sits with his own family and explains his good fortune. He mentions that the mother wants art lessons for the small boy and he has told the mother that his sister is schooled in art and perhaps she might be willing to instruct Da-song. Eager to have the boy occupied, the mother is grateful. And when Ki-woo returns for another lesson, he brings Ki-jung with him. It becomes apparent that the Kims are small-time grifters and they see an opportunity. Dong-ik has a driver. Get rid of him and Ki-woo can recommend Ki-taek for the position. The Parks also have a housekeeper (Lee Jeongeun). Cause her to be released and recommend the Kim mother, Chung–sook (Jang Hye-jin). And within a week or two, the entire Kim family is working for the Parks who are unaaware of the familial connections. It’s at this point that the story takes another turn. The Kims are astonished at their luck, realizing that their sudden wealth and positions are, as Chung-sook says, akin to an iron, which can smooth out all the wrinkles that once plagued them. But of course this is just the middle of act two and when the Parks leave for a long camping weekend, the Kims, of course, take up residence, feeling very much at home, lounging in the living room, food covering the furniture. What could go wrong? Can this charade end well? Writer/director Boon Jong-ho is eager to answer that question, and so the story takes yet another turn that is completely unanticipated. While the family is relaxing, the hour late, the house theirs to enjoy, the doorbell rings. They quickly learn that it’s the recently released housekeeper who has come to retrieve something she insists she left behind when she so hurriedly departed. Beyond this point that it’s best to drop any discussion of plot, for the story again changes, while a strange new twist is introduced. What Parasite does not do is cast either the Kims or the Parks as stereotypes. Each family is in its own way likable and in its own ways insulated by their social and economic situations. Either could have been foils and Joon-ho avoids that trap. How this all unfolds and resolves itself – its startling climax and quiet denouement – represent the true pleasure of watching what proves to be a truly unique and entertaining film. Parasite. Directed by Joon-ho Bong. Starring Song Kang-ho, Jo Jeo-jong and So-dam Park, With subtitles. 2 hrs., 12 min. Rated R.

Movie review by Chris Honoré My Neighbors the Yamadas, written and directed by Isao Takahara and based on a Japanese manga comic strip by Hisachi Ishi, titled Nono-chan, uses an unusual format. It resembles a four or five panel, episodic strip that is told in a series of vignettes which vary in length; each has its own title and deals with a singular issue, such as losing a child in a department store, the relationship between a father and son, the wisdom brought about by age and experience, and the uncertainty of meeting a girlfriend for the first time. The vignettes cover a spectrum of emotions from humor to frustration to heartbreak, demonstrating life’s small conflicts, problems, and joys, all offering an honest picture of the daily routines of a typical middle class Japanese family that resides in urban Tokyo. The family, the Yamadas, consists of a father, Takahashi (James Belushi); mother, Matsuko (Molly Shannon); grandmother, Shige (Tress MacNeille); son, Noboru (Daryl Sabara); and daughter, Nonoko (Lilliana Mumy). Providing a voice-over is David Ogden Stiers. The relationship between Takahashi and Matsuko is the primary focus of the vignettes, the two often disagreeing about the mundane, such as who gets to operate the television remote. Grandma Shige offers the family her wisdom and insights and helpful proverbs, and the children are typical children with their own issues (Noboru is 13; Nonoko is 5). While we see that all of the family members are in some ways flawed, the theme that holds the narrative together is one of familial love and affection. These are kind, decent people. The animation is atypical for a Ghibli feature film. The colors, instead of a vivid and rich palette typical of most of the work produced by the Studio, are soft watercolors that seem closer to simple line drawings. This film offers a nicely crafted window into Japanese family life and culture, which only enriches the story for the western audience. My Neighbors the Yamadas (1999). Animé from Studio Ghibli. Directed by Isao Takahara. With voices of James Belushi, Molly Shannon, Daryl with Sabara, Lilliana Mumy, Tress MacNeille and David Ogden Stiers. Rated PG. 1 hr., 40 min.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré In an article in the New York Times Magazine, director Spike Jonze, when discussing his film, Where the Wild Things Are, said, “Everything we did, all the decisions that we made, were to try to capture the feeling of what it is to be nine.” While it is true that a movie targeting young filmgoers must engage their imaginations and emotions, it shouldn’t necessarily mirror what it feels like to be 9-years-old. At least not completely. There must also be magic and surprise. In other words, this type of film will find more success if it’s a fable that asks young audiences to suspend their disbelief and climb on board – which, of course, they are fully prepared to do. Most likely at the drop of a hat. But first, consider the book. Written by Maurice Sendak and published in 1963, it has sold 19 million copies worldwide, 10 million in the U.S. Its success begs the question what is there about this story that young readers so completely embrace? The story, after all, comprises only 338 words; 41 lines of text; and is only 37 pages long. Perhaps it’s the fact that story is a seamless melding of reality and fantasy. Max, dressed in his wolf costume, consumed with a riptide of emotion, rebels, causing mischief, and is sent to his room. And that’s when the magic begins. His room grows into a forest and he finds a boat and sails to a distant shore where he discovers a band of feral monsters – large, furry, exotic, all strange hybrid animals. He becomes the king of the monsters, wears a crown, carries a scepter, and is empowered. It’s an overwhelming feeling for Max. He stands and yells to the monsters that it’s time to howl and experience their inner wildness. Eventually, however, he decides to return to his family, to those who love him most. Where the Wild Things Are is an elegant and simple story, wonderfully illustrated by Sendak, and one that appeals to any youngster who feels conflicted and perhaps frustrated at being buffeted by the whims of family, school and siblings, who wishes only for a magic place where he can be king. In the first act of the film, Jonze captures with pitch-perfect insight the existential pain of any kid who feels overwhelmed by life. Max (Max Records) is coping with the divorce of his parents, and with a sense of isolation so complete that he talks to fences as if they could talk back. When Max discovers his mother has invited a strange man over for dinner, and sees the nuzzling on the couch, he acts out, argues with his mother and runs from the house, angry and conflicted. It’s at this point that Sendak’s fable begins. This is the real challenge for Jonze as a screenwriter. The difficulty of adapting Sendak’s story to the screen is that it lacks even a semblance of a strong narrative arc. There is only a paper-thin plot, there is no real conflict and there is no resolution. For Sendak’s book to be adapted to the screen as a 98-minute feature, Jonze had to embellish considerably. But by deviating too far from the fable template (and from Sendak’s book), he does so at his peril. Kids wish to be swept up in a story that involves, in some fashion, a journey akin to that found in Shrek or Harry Potter or Spy Kids, one in which the protagonist struggles to overcome adversity, achieves a specific goal, is victorious, and the tale ends with a nice moral. Jonze’s film draws very little from that recipe. The film is imaginative, and the photography superb, with sepia tones in contrast to the crisp, bright colors of most kids’ movies. It could be argued that Where the Wild Things Are is not a film intended for children but for adults who enjoy watching movies that remind them of their childhood. The monsters, which Jonze develops, have names and speak, though they don’t in the book. They are somber and dysfunctional, and Carol (James Gandolfini), the wild thing Max comes to know best, is given to bouts of scary temper, threatening to hurt Max. It’s even suggested that they should eat Max and they’re surprised that they haven’t. Surprisingly, there is no emotional center to the film. Even the relationships between the wild things seem too subtle and strange, something likely to be missed by a younger audience. It’s clear that Jonze made an astonishing effort to adapt a children’s book, but the story simply did not have enough substance to be made into feature film. It was a high-risk gamble by the studio and Jonze. Where the Wild Things Are. Starring Catherine Keener, Max Records, James Gandolfini, Catherine O’Hara, Forest Whitaker and Chris Cooper. Directed by Spike Jonze. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG. Max Records stars in Where the Wild Things Are.

articles.text: Boris Godunov ruled the Tsardom of Russia from 1585 to 1598 and then as the first non-Rurikid tsar from 1598 to 1605. An opera, Boris Godunov, was written about him 200 years later by Modest Mussorgsky. Once upon a time there was a man who thought a lot of himself. He was born to wealth. But that was not enough. He had dreams of greater achievements. As he achieved them, his fame grew also. But that only increased his thirst for power and fame. The young man was clever financially and used his wealth to increase his fame - which also increased his wealth and increased his thirst for power. As his fame and wealth and power increased, they served to feed his ego which also grew and grew. As happens with people like this, fame is not enough by itself. Nor is wealth. It is power that they want. There is a formula that goes something like this: great wealth + ego + the quest for fame = power–hungry megalomania. articles.text: While I know there are folks who have not yet discovered Beaujolais, I have yet to meet someone who dislikes it. It is a charming, fruity, refreshing, early drinking, easy-going wine that goes with tons of foods and is inexpensive. What’s not to like? In many ways it is the opposite of its closest neighbor Burgundy, whose wines are complex, scarce, require serious aging, and cost an arm and a leg. Burgundy was once planted with Pinot Noir and Gamay in roughly the same amounts. In 1395 the Duke of Burgundy decided he didn’t like Gamay and banished it from being planted in Burgundy. So, the Gamay grape migrated to an area just north of Burgundy near the town of Villefranche sur Saone, where it has flourished ever since. The Beaujolais area now produces hundreds of millions of bottles of wine a year and is also, with its green rolling hills, one of the most scenic wine areas to visit. Unlike Burgundy where you have to have an appointment at most places, the Beaujolais vintners have their doors open and welcome drop-in visitors. The two major wine producers in Beaujolais are Louis Jadot and Georges Duboeuf. They are “negociants” who work with hundreds of small farmers to blend and sell their wines. There are 10 villages that make up the heart of Beaujolais – Brouilly, Regnie, Chiroubles, Cote de Brouilly, Fleurie, Saint-Amour, Chenas, Julienas, Morgon, and Moulina-Vent. It is often these names rather than Beaujolais that you will see on the bottle and the name of the Village connotes a step up in quality than regular 2017 Jean-Ernest Descombes Morgon Cote du Py Beaujolais. As mentioned above, Beaujolais goes with a wide variety of foods and is the perfect picnic wine. It is very important to chill the bottle for a half hour in the fridge as its’ not as good at room temperature. I had the opportunity to taste some of the wines of the great Georges Duboeuf. From humble beginnings he has built an empire that sends 30 million bottles of wine all around the world each year. What is stunning about the Duboeuf wines is that even though they are mass produced he retains a very high level of quality. The following wines are ones chosen by Duboeuf from small growers. articles.text: The Piedmont Garden Club, in conjunction with five other Bay Area garden clubs, is sponsoring a webinar that discusses the unique ecological system of the San Francisco Bay. The free webinar will be available on Wednesday, January 13, and will host four Bay Area professors who will discuss flooding, the importance of seaweed, restoration of marshlands, and the need to plant native plants. The event will begin at 9:30 a.m. with an opening slide show. The main program will run from 10 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. Titled “The Power of Plants Will Protect the Bay,” the webinar will describe how scientists are collaborating on ways to protect and restore the Bay shoreline by utilizing plants underwater, in the wetlands, and along the shores. The webinar will feature speakers Karina Nielson, Director of the Estuary and Ocean Science Center, SF State; Dr. Katharyn Boyer, professor of Biology and Wetlands Ecology; Josie Iselin, author of The Curious World of Seaweed; and Diana Benner and Laura Hanson, co-owners of The Watershed Nursery in Richmond. Karina Nielsen, Director of Estuary and Ocean Science Center at San Francisco State University Co-sponsors include Piedmont Garden Club, Woodside-Atherton Garden Club, Marin Garden Club, Hillsborough Garden Club, Orinda Garden Club, and Carmel-By-the-Sea Garden Club. These six organizations are affiliates of the Garden Club of America, whose mission is to “restore, improve and protect the quality of the environment through educational programs and action in the fields of conservation and civic improvement.” Pre-registration for the event is required. articles.text: There are two major types of quality port – Vintage and Tawny. Vintage port is bottled early and left to mature in the bottles, something that takes a long time. If you buy a bottle of the current vintage port (2017) it may not be ready to drink for 10 years. For those of us who are getting up in years, this can be a problem. There is a solution however: tawny port. Tawny port is left in the barrels at the winery to age anywhere from 10 to 40 years. So, when it is released it is totally ready to drink with no further aging required. Its time in barrel turns the wine from dark purple to a tawny golden brown, hence the name. This beautiful wine starts slow and builds to a nice crescendo, with the acidity emerging to cut the fruit. This elegant wine has a semi-sweet finish to go with its vibrancy and energy. It’s a pretty picture overall with caramel, molasses and hints of chocolate on the finish. This wine cries out for a bowl of cashews, a nice pipe and a roaring fire.

articles.text: Even in these unprecedented times, the Piedmont Avenue Branch is running smoothly. That it is even open in the face of the daunting challenge of COVID-19 is testimony to the spirit, ingenuity, persistence, and commitment of the four people who make it happen – Emily, Hana, Nikki and Colette. Three of them work inside and one is at the outside table from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. five days a week, Tuesday through Saturday. Inside the library they collect the books that are returned to the Echo Avenue receptacles, take them inside and spread them out on a table where the books stay for at least 24 hours before being put on shelves. They also receive books delivered by Oakland Public Library’s van, and process those books immediately. The books were held in quarantine before OPL delivered them to the branch. Inside workers check email requests, find the right books and package them in a bag with the patron’s name. When the patron arrives outside, a worker calls the inside desk on a walkie-talkie and the bag with the order is brought outside. On a recent day, Jenera Burton, the branch librarian a few years ago and now the Supervising Librarian for West and North Oakland, was visiting the Piedmont Avenue library to see how things are going. Dear Abby A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets Terrific tales for rainy days By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: Golden Gate Labrador Retriever Rescue will hold a virtual pet fair this Saturday, January 9, starting at 11:00 a.m. It will allow prospective adopters to see the Labs we have up for adoption and find out about the adoption process. To learn a little about these dogs before the fair, check out our website at labrescue.org where you can also register for Saturday’s Virtual Fair. We wish we could do this in person, but this is nice alternative. Hope you come and sniff out a great Lab for your family. – Cherry, a volunteer at Golden Gate Rescue Dear Cherry: Thanks so much for letting us know. A virtual fair sounds like an excellent alternative for getting a decent idea of a dog that needs to meet a kind family. As I understand it, if you’re certain you want to adopt, adopters stand a much better chance of getting a Lab if they donate a non-refundable $400 adoption fee, fill out an application and talk to a representative about what they are looking for in a dog: male, female, weight, age, training, hair, etc. Golden Gate Labrador Retriever Rescue’s review of applications takes a few days, but you don’t need to apply before the Lab Fair. Simply register. I saw some very good-looking canine candidates on the website – Charley, Maizie, Paige and Tank. They are definitely worth a look. Wagging our tails for Golden Gate Rescue, –Abby Dear Abby: We are going stir crazy in this rain. Do you have any good dog or cat movies that might be fun to watch for a Family Night? Woof, –Tracey, Tom, the kids and Bucko Dear Tracey, Tom, kids and Bucko: There’s always the “Golden Dog Films” of the past: Old Yeller, Lassie and The Incredible Journey, which never fail to capture my dog heart regardless of how many times I’ve seen them. And, from the kennels of history, Wendy and Lucy, Sounder and Megan Leavey are also great tales of dog lives and escapes. If you’re interested in animation, Walt Disney’s Balto or The Fox and the Hound are worth a try. My personal favorite is the original 101 Dalmatians. The newer Dalmatian versions are good, too, but there’s nothing like the original. If you want to see tear-jerkers, there’s Marley and Me or Hachi: A Dog’s Tale. They should positively get everyone howling. But the magical series Wallace & Gromit is always good for a lot of laughs, and the stop-motion wonders of Isle of Dogs or Frankenweenie, which are positively great. If you’ve seen all of those, take a peek at Cujo or White Dog – they are tales of dogs that could use a bit of obedience training… Imagine that. Hope one of these wags your tails, –Abby Piedmont Ave. Library – 2021 Update In November, we reported that Oakland Public Library was beginning to plan and to negotiate with the union, steps necessary for opening branches in early 2021. Unfortunately, the recent surge in COVID-19 cases in Alameda County has thrown a wrench in those plans, and while the library continues to plan for “inside services,” there is no estimated date for allowing the public inside the libraries according to OPL Director Jamie Turbak. Oakland Public Library continues to provide many services and programs for the community, including sidewalk pick up, rain or shine, and a new children’s services program – Winter Bingo. Winter Bingo is a fun family literacy game recommended for kids up to age 12. To play Winter, visit our sidewalk pick up to collect a Winter Bingo card, or download one from the OPL website. Friends of Piedmont Avenue Library We continue to work toward securing a permanent home for the Piedmont Avenue Branch. The Friends of PAL will continue to monitor and support Oakland Public Library’s efforts to lease the former Child Development Center at Piedmont Avenue Elementary School from the school district, which owns the building. If the branch library could be housed in that building, it would triple the available space for activities and events. The next virtual meeting of Friends of PAL is scheduled for Tuesday, January 12, at 7pm. Look for a notice with Zoom instructions. Updates from the county, as they relate to the Piedmont Avenue branch library, will be posted on the web site, friendsofpal.org. How Piedmont Ave. Library functions during pandemic By Ruby Long Even in these unprecedented times, the Piedmont Avenue Branch is running smoothly. That it is even open in the face of the daunting challenge of COVID-19 is testimony to the spirit, ingenuity, persistence, and commitment of the four people who make it happen – Emily, Hana, Nikki and Colette. Three of them work inside and one is at the outside table from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. five days a week, Tuesday through Saturday. Inside the library they collect the books that are returned to the Echo Avenue receptacles, take them inside and spread them out on a table where the books stay for at least 24 hours before being put on shelves. They also receive books delivered by Oakland Public Library’s van, and process those books immediately. The books were held in quarantine before OPL delivered them to the branch. Inside workers check email requests, find the right books and package them in a bag with the patron’s name. When the patron arrives outside, a worker calls the inside desk on a walkie-talkie and the bag with the order is brought outside. On a recent day, Jenera Burton, the branch librarian a few years ago and now the Supervising Librarian for West and North Oakland, was visiting the Piedmont Avenue library to see how things are going. She said that the librarians in all the branches miss having regular contact with patrons. Ruby Long is a neighbor whose work has appeared in local and national publications. All information above is from The Hoot, the newsletter of Piedmont Avenue Library. Subscription is free. To subscribe, go to: https://www.friendsofpal.org/news.htm. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

Linda Beach A master plan was adopted by city council in 2017 to redesign parts of Linda Beach Playfield, adjacent to Beach Elementary School, and to install a new “playscape” in the park. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) also donated $100,000 to help assist with the project, with a particular emphasis on the Tot Lot. “These funds help the city really start thinking seriously about [moving forward] with the master plan,” Nakahara said. A ceremonial check was presented by former PBF president Patty Siskind to Lillevand at the city’s Tree Lighting ceremony on December 2. articles.text: What can you do to fill time while you’re responsibly sheltering in place? Write poetry Yes, poetry. And here’s a famous example to get you started: A tutor who tooted the flute Tried to tutor two tooters to toot. Said the two to the tutor, “Is it harder to toot or To tutor two tooters to toot?” Yep, it’s a limerick, that unique five-line form that will never challenge the sonnet for versatility, but which can make us smile. It can also provide plenty of chances for writers to show what they can do. Here’s one I did yesterday: A limerick is a big cinch to write. No problem, no poetic fright. Only pen lines one and two. Just three more to do Ogden Nash it’s not, but I had fun putting it together, so in the spirit of fun I challenge all Piedmonters to have fun, too—to fashion their own limericks and to submit them to the Post. The challenge is a friendly one, with no winners or losers. In a way you’ll be challenging yourself, and you’ll be doing your part to cheer up your town. So, give it a try. Here are three more from me to get you started: A fussy food critic named Willy Thought that noshing sushi was silly Raw fish on a plate Was nothing he ate But he scarfed steak tartare willy-nilly. A virus named Vern hit the air. An explosive sneeze blew him there. But with no host around, He fell to the ground, Crying, “Darn it all, life isn’t fair!” A plucky newspaper, the Post Refused to give up the ghost.
